body:
I received some feedback that the horizon isn't bright enough and I agree with this, I'm going to tweak this a bit more along with the sky colour. I'm concerned this won't work well for a dark sky (night time), though... Maybe instead of a brightness multiplication I can have it be exponential or something.

There is also some concern that a more saturated blue sky colour will contribute too much blue to the ambient light. This is because in a normal scene, there are surfaces that are reflecting the direct (white) light from the sun in all directions, which make the overall ambient light appear less blue. The ground is also often in direct sunlight and much brighter than the colour used here, which also adds a bunch of non-blue indirect light that makes the ambient light less blue. I'm not sure what to do about this. In terms of a single model floating in space, the current behaviour of having blue ambient light looks good. But when you start putting a real scene in place, this ambient light no longer makes sense.

One option might be to change the ambient light sky contribution to be lower, but this does not affect reflected light. I think the discrepancy between reflected light and ambient light makes changing the sky contribution a non-option.

In terms of a physical simulation, nothing about this is physical. Chasing physical correctness is something I have no interest in because it's all wrong (even setting a sky colour makes no sense because the sky doesn't have a strong "albedo" in reality -- it's mostly about how much different frequencies of light scatter.) This is why the PR just does simple colour math, just like Godot has always done.

Let me know if you have any thoughts!

For context of people reading: Allen and I have had some back and forth in DMs. My priority is to ensure that these settings don't negatively affect the consistency of how assets look when imported in different engines (unity, unreal, Godot). Assets should look "right" out of the box. We've had issues in the past (Godot3) where the default scene would just have ambient and no directional light in editor, and every asset had a very distinct blue-ish tint. People have complained for a long time and opened threads over threads asking "why is Godot making my assets blue". 

I would like to see some before/after comparison with a simple scene with white geometry (a cube on a plane).

Did a few variations. (Default Materials - default MeshInstance3D material when no override is set. Custom Materials - Default material when you create a new material, which I think the only difference of is that the albedo color is fully white instead of very slightly gray-ish, didn't do any edits otherwise. AgX is left at default parameters.) | / | Default Materials + Linear Tonemapping | Custom Materials + Linear Tonemapping | Default Materials + AgX | Custom Materials + AgX | | - | - | - | - | - | |Old| | | | | |New| | | | |

I've realized that, although the current horizon colour maths in this PR may improve on the existing maths, there are some fundamental problems that need to be addressed either with some hacky fixes or an overhaul of the approach. I've marked this as a draft to signify that it's not worth really testing thoroughly just yet.
